slide.title: Many Trees Beat One
slide.body: Left: many small trees side by side (forest). Right: a chain of small trees, each fixing the last (boosting). Tag: Machine Learning with scikit-learn · Lesson 12.

scenes.on_screen_text: What if we combine many trees?
scenes.voiceover: One decision tree is easy to understand, but unstable. Change a few rows, and it can grow very differently. What if you trained hundreds of trees and combined them? That simple idea is behind two of the strongest model families for business data.

slide.title: Random forest
slide.body: Data → many random samples → many deep trees (each sees random features) → average (regression) or vote (classification).

scenes.voiceover: An ensemble combines many models into one prediction. The first approach is a random forest. It trains many deep trees, each on a random sample of the rows, and each looking at a random subset of features at every split. So each tree makes different mistakes.

slide.title: Why forests overfit less
slide.body: Averaging cancels each tree's noise · Key settings: n_estimators, max_depth, min_samples_leaf, max_features · n_jobs=-1 trains trees in parallel

scenes.voiceover: For regression, the forest averages the trees' predictions. For classification, it combines their votes. Averaging cancels out much of each tree's noise, so a forest overfits much less than one deep tree. The trees are independent, so they can train in parallel.

slide.title: Gradient boosting
slide.body: Tree 1 → errors → Tree 2 fixes them → remaining errors → Tree 3 … Final prediction = sum of all trees.

scenes.voiceover: The second approach is gradient boosting. It trains small trees one after another. Each new tree tries to correct the errors the earlier trees still make. It is often the most accurate model on tables of data, but it has more settings, and it can overfit if it runs too long.

slide.title: A sensible order
slide.body: 1. Simple baseline (linear or logistic) · 2. Random forest: strong with defaults · 3. HistGradientBoosting: best accuracy, more tuning · No scaling needed for trees

scenes.voiceover: scikit-learn has fast versions, called histogram gradient boosting. They group values into bins, handle missing values without an imputer, and can stop early. Neither ensemble needs scaled features, because both are built from trees. Start with a simple baseline, try a random forest next, then boosting when you want the best accuracy.

scenes.stock_query: glass jar full of beans on table
scenes.voiceover: Ask one person to guess the number of beans in a jar, and the guess may be far off. Ask two hundred people and average their guesses, and the average is often closer. A random forest is that crowd. Boosting is a team where each new member fixes what the team got wrong so far.

scenes.stock_query: electric scooters parked city street Africa
scenes.voiceover: Amara Diallo runs analytics for a scooter-rental start-up in Dakar, Senegal. She has the same kind of hourly demand problem as lesson eleven, and wants to know if ensembles are worth their extra complexity.

screen_steps: Scroll past the L11 setup and model cells, already executed.

Type this exact code cell from content.md and run it with Shift+Enter:
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, HistGradientBoostingRegressor

cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
models = {"linear": LinearRegression(),
          "forest": RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, n_jobs=-1, random_state=0),
          "boosting": HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0)}
for name, model in models.items():
    rmse = -cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=cv,
                            scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
    print(f"{name:8} RMSE={rmse.mean():.1f} (std {rmse.std():.1f})")
scenes.voiceover: We continue in the bike notebook, with the training data ready. This cell creates five folds, then cross-validates three models on the same folds: linear regression, a forest of two hundred trees, and gradient boosting. For each, it prints the mean RMSE and the spread.

screen_steps: Highlight the minus sign before cross_val_score and scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error".
scenes.voiceover: Two details. scikit-learn scores follow the rule that higher is better, so errors come back as negative numbers. The minus sign at the start turns them into normal RMSE values. And we use plain folds, not stratified ones, because the target is a number.

screen_steps: Highlight the three output lines: linear RMSE=182.3 (std 2.8), forest RMSE=128.7 (std 1.6), boosting RMSE=122.6 (std 1.8).
scenes.voiceover: The results. Linear regression has an RMSE of one hundred and eighty-two point three, with a spread of two point eight. The forest scores one hundred and twenty-eight point seven, spread one point six. Boosting scores one hundred and twenty-two point six, spread one point eight.

screen_steps: Add the overlay: ensembles about 50+ bikes/hour better than linear.
Add a text cell: Choice: gradient boosting. Next: better features.
scenes.voiceover: Both ensembles cut the error by more than fifty bikes per hour, far more than the spread. Boosting is about six bikes per hour better than the forest, also more than the spread. So Amara picks gradient boosting. But all three models still see only temperature, humidity and hour.

A common mistake is to assume the most complex model always wins, and skip the baseline. On small or noisy data, a simple linear model can match an untuned ensemble. Always compare with a baseline on the same folds. And do not forget the minus sign on error scores.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Random forest: averages trees, overfits less. 2. Gradient boosting: trees fix earlier errors; HistGradientBoosting is fast. 3. Same folds, simple baseline, mind the minus sign.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, a random forest averages many different trees, which reduces overfitting, so it is a strong, low-effort second model. Second, gradient boosting adds trees one by one to correct earlier errors, and the histogram versions are fast and handle missing values. Third, compare ensembles with a simple baseline on the same folds, and remember that error scores are negative in scikit-learn.
